procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention passed by the District Magistrate on October 24, 1971, under sections 3(2) and 5 of the Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a Writ Petition (No. 195 of 1972) in the Supreme Court under its original jurisdiction challenging the detention order. The Supreme Court allowed the respondents to file an affidavit on the point of whether the petitioner was in custody on the date the detention order was passed. The petition was ultimately dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be legally made against a person who is already in custody on the date of the making of such order.

facts: The petitioner's lawyer contended that the detention order, made on October 24, 1971, was illegal because the petitioner was already in custody since his arrest on October 6, 1971.
law: The court considered the petitioner's argument to be an "abstract proposition of law".
application: The court found it unnecessary to rule on the legal question of whether a detention order can be made against someone already in custody.
This was because the court determined that, as a matter of fact, the petitioner was not in custody on October 24, 1971, when the detention order was actually made.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument by refuting its factual basis. Since the court found that the petitioner was not actually in custody when the detention order was issued, it did not have to decide the legal question of whether such an order would have been valid if he had been.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure of the State Government to specify the period of detention in the order confirming the detention introduces an infirmity in the detention.

law.fact_text: Section 12(1) of the Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act 1964 states that if the Advisory Board reports sufficient cause for detention, the government may confirm the order and continue the detention for a period it thinks fit.
Section 13 of the Act specifies a maximum detention period of two years from the date of detention.
Section 13(2) of the Act gives the government the power to revoke or modify a detention order at any time before the maximum period expires.
A precedent set in Ujagar Singh v. The State of the Punjab held that the non-specification of a definite period in a detention order was not a material omission that would render the order invalid.

application.fact_text: The Court interpreted the language of Section 12(1) and found nothing that requires the government to specify the detention period when confirming the order. The phrase "for such period as it thinks fit" is seen as a consequence of the confirmation, not a requirement to be stated within it.

The Court reasoned that it is not always practical or feasible for the government to specify the period at the time of confirmation. The decision to continue detention depends on various factors and future events, and the government needs flexibility.

The Court noted that the detention is not indefinite, as it is capped by the two-year maximum period established in Section 13. The government's power to revoke the order early provides an additional safeguard.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention, holding that the failure to specify the period of detention in the confirmation order does not invalidate the detention. The Court based this decision on its interpretation of the Act, which does not mandate such a specification, the practical need for governmental flexibility, and the existence of a statutory maximum detention period.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be legally made against a person who is already in custody on the date of the making of such order.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner was arrested on October 6, 1971, and was therefore already in custody when the detention order was made against him on October 24, 1971.
A detention order cannot legally be made against a person who is already in custody on the date of the order.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner was not in custody on October 24, 1971, when the detention order was made.
The petitioner was taken into custody on the same day the detention order was passed, not before.

cases.case_name: Ujagar Singh v. The State of the Punjab
cases.principle: The non-specification of any definite period in a detention order was not a material omission that would render the order invalid.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When confirming a detention order under section 12 of the Act, the government is not legally required to also specify the period of detention.
obiter: It is not always practicable and feasible for the State Government at the time of confirming the detention order to specify the period of detention.

The court will not express an opinion on the abstract legal proposition of whether a detention order can be made against a person who is already in custody if the facts of the case show the person was not in custody when the order was made.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court dismissed the petition by first resolving a factual dispute, finding that the petitioner was not already in custody when the detention order was made, which rendered it unnecessary to decide the abstract legal question of whether such an order could be validly issued against a person already in custody. The court further held that the failure of the State Government to specify the period of detention in its confirmation order does not invalidate the detention, as the governing statute does not impose such a requirement, and practical considerations regarding evolving circumstances make it unfeasible to fix a period at the time of confirmation.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of Section 12 of the Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964, to determine if it requires the government to specify the period of detention in a confirmation order.

Reliance on precedent, specifically the case of Ujagar Singh v. The State of the Punjab, which held that non-specification of a definite period in a detention order is not a material omission that would render the order invalid.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the petitioner's factual premise for his first argument, finding that he was not in custody on October 24, 1971, when the order for his detention was made.
The court found that the plain language of Section 12 of the Act does not enjoin upon the State Government the duty to specify the period of detention when confirming a detention order.
The court relied on the precedent set in Ujagar Singh v. The State of the Punjab, which established that non-specification of a detention period is not a material omission that invalidates the order.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's factual position that the petitioner was not in custody on the date the detention order was passed, thereby negating the petitioner's primary legal challenge.
The court's interpretation of Section 12 of the Act supported the respondent's actions, concluding that the law only requires the government to confirm the order, not to specify its duration.

The court accepted the practical argument that the government needs flexibility to assess the appropriate length of detention based on evolving circumstances, rather than being forced to specify a period at the outset.
policy_considerations: it is not always practicable and feasible for the State Government at the time of confirming the detention order to specify the period of detention.

The continued detention of the detenu, subject to the maximum period prescribed by the Act, depends upon a variety of factors and the State Government would have to take into account all the circumstances including fresh developments and subsequent events in deciding whether to keep the detenu in detention for the maximum period or to release him.
